title: I'm a marketing guy, not a dev. Built a full game with AI over a few months. Here's what actually broke.
author: Scooscoo5000
selftext:
I've wanted to make a game since I was a kid. Never learned to code properly, can't draw. Went into marketing instead and figured that was that, until AI got good enough that the gap stopped mattering. A few months later there's a real game with real people playing it, which still feels strange to type.

The game is DigMorph, a creature collector where you build a trap, bait it, and hunt things to fill a dex. 34 regions, each with its own mechanic, plus a roguelite wave mode. That's the context. The part worth talking about here is what building this way was actually like, because the answer isn't "AI wrote it and it worked."

What I didn't expect: AI removed the bottleneck on writing code, so I built far more game than I could personally verify. And everything that broke, broke silently. Three from the last week alone.

**My player stats were completely fake and I didn't notice for months.** One account showed 716 play sessions when it had really had 5. The aggregator counted events every time they arrived, but my client retries failed batches, so every retry recounted. It also kept a running total in memory and wrote the whole record back, so two servers running at once overwrote each other. Two bugs pulling in opposite directions, some numbers way too high, others too low. Then after fixing all that it still kept climbing, because a totally different part of the code was adding a session every single time the game autosaved. Three separate causes for one wrong number, written at different times, each one perfectly reasonable on its own.

**My game promised players something it never delivered.** There's a mechanic whose tutorial text literally says "guaranteed catch." The code checked whether a value was 200 or higher to trigger it. That check assumed the base was 100. The actual config said 32, so the number could never get there. Players did everything right and got a coin flip instead of the guarantee. Nothing errored. It just quietly lied for months.

**My crash reporting had never worked once.** The game dutifully caught every crash and sent it to my server. The server had a list of allowed event types and crash reports were never added to it, so it silently binned all of them. I had a lovely empty error dashboard that I read as "no crashes." It actually meant "no data."

The pattern is identical every time. AI is great at the happy path. It's bad at retries, at two servers running at once, at remembering that a number in file A has to match a number in file B. It'll confidently write both sides of a boundary weeks apart and never notice they don't line up. None of this threw an error. It all just quietly did the wrong thing while looking healthy.

One more, and this one stings. I had AI write my trailer copy and it put "34 Hand-Painted Worlds" on screen. My art is a mix of licensed asset packs and AI generated pieces. It is not hand painted. I didn't catch it, I posted it, and I got publicly called out for lying about my own game. I wasn't lying, I just shipped a claim I never checked. AI will assert things about your project that it has no way to know, and marketing copy is the worst possible place for that, because that's the part people screenshot. Trailer's fixed as of today. Lesson learned in the most public way available.

What actually works: I'm useful now in a way I wasn't before, but not as a programmer. The real job turned out to be deciding what should exist and then not trusting that it works until I've watched it work. All the time went into design, systems and balance. That part is entirely mine, and it's the only part AI couldn't do for me.

Game's here if you want to poke at it. Free, browser, no download, closed beta with 17 regions open, feedback button in game.

[https://dig-morph-rose.vercel.app](https://dig-morph-rose.vercel.app/)

Genuinely curious if others building this way hit the same wall, where writing the code is never the problem but nothing ever tells you when it's quietly wrong. What's your process for catching that?

i have posted in other communities and all the comment i have got were it's made with ai it's garbage but this will ne discourage me as i have put a lot of time on this mainly to learn but the result was a game that i have massively enjoyed myself.

replies.author: DoNotUseThisInMyHome
replies.body: True. I laughed so badly in this post.

comments.author: Reckonerxy
comments.body:
Capturing concept looks pretty similar to my own game I'm working on. Got some questions.  
\-Are you planning to keep the AI art for the monsters? I think it's okay as a proof of concept but showing AI art to real players might be a turn off.  
\-When I tried to check out the game it ask me to sign in. Is that really necessary for the prototype, that might make things harder for other people to trying out your game.



https://preview.redd.it/z2q5z5znpldh1.png?width=1388&format=png&auto=webp&s=b3e2d016a1c4dccb34c816345f3d2128a09cbe7c

replies.author: Scooscoo5000
replies.body:
thanks for your answer, no im not planning to keep the ai art for monster, i had a deal with a very talented artist but he ghosted me, also looked for assets packs but nothing matches the vision ive had for the game.

as for the login, it's really necessary as i want to avoid spammers and people using scripts, i'm using clerk and it's a very credible login management platform and i only collect email addresses and nothing else.

replies.author: Reckonerxy
replies.body: I think is more important that you give more accessibility to people willing your game, rather that worrying about spammers, as a login screen is really big point of friction, specially if your game is still early in development.

replies.author: Scooscoo5000
replies.body: it's pretty much a complete game minus the art that is still pending, and also to be honest this is to gather a list of people i can notify when the game is out, and most people have throw away accounts just for this reason to login in games and websites but i still understand your point of view and it's 100% legitimate

replies.author: Scooscoo5000
replies.body: you can play it on your desktop or mobile browser : [https://dig-morph-rose.vercel.app](https://dig-morph-rose.vercel.app/)

comments.author: teamharder
comments.body: I'm glad you enjoyed making the game, but I wouldn't expect a warm reception anywhere. Do people actually play this for any meaningful amount of time? Sorry to be negative, it's hard to imagine why.

replies.author: Scooscoo5000
replies.body: yes i have around 20 people active on the game especially coming for a community called r/mousehunt which is a great game i took inspiration from and added my own twist, and yeah i have received countless downvotes and negative comments but it does not bother me in the slightest, this is my first experience in game dev and it's been a blast to play and build the game.

replies.author: promptling
replies.body: Twenty active players is enough to stop guessing. I’d watch five first sessions and tag four moments: trap built, bait placed, first catch, and reason for leaving. If most reach one catch but don’t return, test a visible next-region tease before adding more content. I’m building [Patchloop](https://patchloop.io/) for AI built WIPs; DigMorph could use a dedicated room to turn that small cohort into a repeatable feedback loop.

replies.author: Scooscoo5000
replies.body: Thanks for the precious feedback im analysing telemetry every day so far it’s been rough but im adjusting as i go, will take a look at it Patchloop sounds interesting.

comments.author: aberroco
comments.body:
Well, it fails exactly as expected, because AI can't engineer software, can't make a viable decision, can't see consequences and can't remember the code base, every time you run it all it sees is a system prompt, your client's system prompt (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md or alike + memory + whatever your app feeds it), past conversation in the current chat and your prompt. After which it just uses text finding tools to gather info how the project works. Fine for something small. Breaks down the closer when the project grows.

No, I don't hit the same wall, I do use AI in code generation, but I have understanding what it should do and verify everything it does (ok, almost everything - I do vibe-code tests, because they change too frequently to meaningfully verify them every time; and I know I wouldn't write tests myself if I would be writing without AI assistance, so vibe-coded tests beat no tests). After debugging yesterday I see it did solved the issue, but not in the way I expected, so today I spend a couple hours figuring out why (I was wrong in my assumptions what should be done) and finding another way with cleaner API. 

I couldn't count how many times AI's approach was anywhere from ugly to completely inappropriate and invalid. But it does what it's supposed to do, just without much regards to things it shouldn't do, or things it might need to do in the future. It's like trying to do a skyscraper without planning. Pour foundation for eh... "big building", make support columns (no specs; no load bearing calculations). There's cracks at the bottom floor's walls? Just install windows - they'd provide additional support. The load is heavily off-centered on one side? Just... add some straps at the other side. You might guess what would happen with such "architectural approach".

replies.author: Scooscoo5000
replies.body: i get your point but i might want to add that i have studied basic code during my marketing years and i also have decent workflows i use in my 9-5 job which helped build some very useful small apps to automate 60% of the work we do.

replies.author: aberroco
replies.body:
Basic code is exactly what AI can do. It's like learning a new programming language. Any SWE can do this in a week, that's not what SWE is about. Decisions are. Knowing good patters, understanding architecture of the project, understanding how your changes might affect other parts, how everything works together, etc. 

>small apps

Exactly what I said. It works for small apps, with limited scope and codebase. Once your codebase passes about 100k lines (which is still relatively small project) it starts to fail. 1M lines - it mostly fails, unless properly harnessed, directed and verified.

replies.author: FridgeBaron
replies.body: its crazy how many times I'll glance at its thoughts and what its planning is insane. Obviously I also miss it but yeah some choices are just like what the hell?

replies.author: teamharder
replies.body: With Fable and Opus 4.8, why the focus on the ability to code? Who cares how its written if there are zero bugs and it performs well. Youre making games, not financial or medical software. Having some basic gamedev concept knowledge (e.g. pooling) helps so you know what to call out, but I firmly believe you can make a solid game with zero programming code knowledge at this point.

replies.author: aberroco
replies.body:
Good luck with that, thinking game development is nothing compared to medical or financial software. 

Btw, my last job was in medical. And it was mindnumbingly boring, compared to the previous place in training simulation software, or the current game I'm working on.

replies.author: teamharder
replies.body: Im saying its low stakes. Nobody is going to die becuase its not perfectly architected. There's no breaking some sort of financial or medical privacy law. It's a piece of software you have fun with. The worst you can do is ruin a fun experience. It's not that serious.

comments.author: Scooscoo5000
comments.body:
EDIT : 

Hey, thanks for trying DigMorph. Hope you got at least a bit of fun out of it.

First round of testing wraps today. Testers turned up some real problems, including a couple of bugs that were quietly ending runs, and those are all fixed now. Round two is coming shortly with a lot more of the map open and a new region.

If you have a minute, the one thing that would help me most: what made you stop playing? Bug, boredom, confusion, or just life getting busy, all of it is useful. Blunt is fine, I'd rather hear it than not.

Thanks again for the time.
